h: An Admiral's Fortune and a Park Full of Follies
p: Much of the Anson family's money came from George Anson, the naval commander who sailed round the world in the 1740s and captured a Spanish treasure galleon along the way. That prize helped his brother Thomas transform Shugborough, and the house and parkland you see today owe a lot to that seafaring windfall. The family later became Earls of Lichfield, which is how photographer Patrick Lichfield fits into the story.

The monuments scattered through the park are a treat to hunt down. Several were designed by James 'Athenian' Stuart, who was obsessed with ancient Greece, including a Triumphal Arch, the Tower of the Winds and a Doric temple, while the Chinese House reflects the family's links with the East. Give yourselves time and a map, as they're spread out.
Allow at least half a day. The site is large, so comfortable footwear makes a big difference.

Don't leave without seeing the Essex Bridge, the long medieval packhorse bridge that crosses the River Trent at the edge of the estate near Great Haywood. Its narrow, many-arched span is wonderfully photogenic. Nearby, Great Haywood Junction is where the Trent and Mersey Canal meets the Staffordshire and Worcestershire Canal, a lovely place to watch narrowboats come and go. In Stafford, the Ancient High House, a striking Tudor timber-framed townhouse, and the hilltop ruins of Stafford Castle are both worth a look.
